newsitem.title: USA: Kaiser Aluminum starts-up new micro-mill.
newsitem.headline: Kaiser Aluminum starts-up new micro-mill.

text.p: Kaiser Aluminum Corp has started what it terms the industry's first micro-mill to produce cansheet at half the operating cost of traditional mills, the company said.
Kaiser's micro-mill in Reno, Nev. came on stream two weeks ago, ahead of schedule, and has a capacity to produce 100 million pounds (45,359 tonnes) of cansheet.
Reno will also make tab and end stock.
Cansheet accounts for a quarter of the world's aluminum consumption.
Ray Milchovich, President of Kaiser flat rolled products and micro-mills, said Reno's role will be to research and refine micro-mill technology and be a showcase.
"We are very happy with the progress. We are casting regularly and going through the normal start up," Milchovich said. "We intend to sell product in 1997."
Traditionally molten aluminum is cast into slab which is rolled many times to make thin sheet for beverage cans.
Mini-mills were later developed to cast molten scrap directly into sheet which is rolled thinner.
Kaiser said with its micro-mill, molten metal is cast directly into thin strip and coiled in one step, thereby saving money and time.

"We can build a micro-mill to make body stock only for about $45 million to make 100 million pounds a year," Milchovich said. "We anticipate the operating costs will be half of the average cost of running a traditional rolling mill."
The micro-mill can use primary aluminum or scrap.

Robert Unger of Planned Technology Associates of New Jersey, a company specializing in casting technology, said that with a high scrap feed, Kaiser's micro-mill has an operating advantage of 4 to 5 cents per pound compared to larger, DC cast conventional mills.

Kaiser is targetting Latin America and the Far East for micro-mill sales. "In the devloping world you have double digit growth in cansheet usage, and we anticipate double digit growth for the next 10 to 15 years," Milchovich said.

Kaiser will face tough competition in the Far East from Alcoa's established canstock making venture with Kobe which some believe has already eaten into markets served by U.S. rivals Alumax and Commonwealth Aluminum.
Alcoa is also active in Eastern and Western Europe.
Kaiser said it was not aiming to build any more mirco-mills in the U.S. which is already a net exporter of cansheet.

But Unger said Kaiser's micro-mill strip, reported at 13 inches wide, is too narrow and knocks the company out of the canbody sheet market in North America and many developing markets. The strip may have to be widened to make it more competitive, he said.
"Larger multi-national canmaking companies operating in overseas markets will want wider lines in their factories from what we have been able to determine," Unger said.
Milchovich said, "I think any canmaker will be able to take the micro-mill strip and make cans," though he conceded there "may need to be customised canmaking technology."
Milchovich added that Kaiser was developing its own canmaking technology which will be patented next year.
